newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia PM refuses to rule out tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Australia PM refuses to rule out tax reform.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Tuesday explicitly refused to rule out any future reform of the tax system, a day after a poll showed the controversial proposal for a consumption tax was a vote winner.

"He said 'I'm not prepared to rule out altogether any future reform of the taxation system'," a spokesman for the ruling Liberal-National Party coalition quoted Howard as telling a meeting of government parliamentarians.
But Howard said any reforms would have to lead to job creation, a lifting of exports, enhance living standards and encourage national savings, the spokesman said.
On Monday, the Bulletin newsweekly's Morgan poll showed 59 percent of voters it surveyed now favoured a New Zealand-style goods and services tax (GST), compared with 56 percent a year ago.
The poll found those who opposed it had dropped to 31 percent from 37 percent a year earlier.
A GST is a consumption tax paid by consumers when they buy a good or service.

Howard said last week he believed that tax reform debate was needed, leaving the way open for the coalition government to adopt a GST policy in the lead-up to the next election, due to be held by early 1999.
The coalition was widely perceived to have lost a general election in 1993 because of a strenuous Labor campaign against its plans to introduce a GST, combined with lower income taxes.
It ousted the 13-year-old Labor administration in March 1996 after dropping the tax proposal and pledging not to introduce a GST in its first term.

But it has not ruled out such a tax in later terms and support for a GST is escalating with even welfare groups, which opposed the 1993 plan, now calling for an overhaul of a complex tax system that relies heavily on income taxes and is marked by high marginal rates of up to 47 percent.
Australia also has a range of indirect taxes, including sales tax, that are applied patchily and at varying rates.
